prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The American common is no collective or princedom but privacies of need & pleasure as they intersect in public spaces, tho the insufferable powers that be breed their plots behind our backs, thinking us witless, seemingly blind to their afflicted intentions, just a bunch of demographic motormouths & screw-ups to be targeted by commodities traders & search engines— a marketing niche for every need, stereotypes tagged by algorithms—here is a typical team of baton twirlers in an airport bar, each of them clad in foxy red track suits & tuned-in to the dollhouse stimulations of pigeon-talking sales reps; there is a previously undetected aggregation of retirees, evangelical camp kids, kickass bowlers, and mothy nuns in starched wimples, for whom the news of the day means the aging boy-man Hugh Grant's fear of double chins—neither of these or any other data dump entirely false, but so narrow-minded sometimes as to lose sight of us entirely: the midtown lady in Capris, a four-square surgeon off-duty & headed out to play poker, the plumber fly-fishing by the river— a sky of twilight slate now—not a word written on it.

outputs.L1: The American common is neither a collective nor a princedom, but a constellation of private needs and pleasures as they intersect in public spaces. Yet the insufferable powers that be hatch their plots behind our backs, taking us for witless, seemingly blind to their afflicted intentions: merely a swarm of demographic motormouths and screw-ups to be targeted by commodities traders and search engines—a marketing niche for every need, stereotypes tagged by algorithms. outputs.L2: The American public is not a single body or a realm ruled from above, but a patchwork of private wants and pleasures meeting in shared places. Meanwhile, the unbearable authorities hatch their schemes out of sight, assuming we are foolish, as if they cannot see the damage in their own designs, reducing us to talkative demographic clusters and misfits fit only to be pursued by commodity dealers and search engines—every desire assigned its market segment, every stereotype labeled by an algorithm. Here, for instance, is an ordinary group of baton twirlers in an airport lounge, all dressed in sharp red tracksuits and absorbed in the miniature excitements offered by chattering sales representatives. Over there is some newly noticed cluster of retirees, evangelical summer-camp children, formidable bowlers, and dusty nuns in stiff white wimples, people for whom today’s headlines amount to the aging boyish Hugh Grant worrying about developing a double chin. None of these groupings, nor any other pile of data, is wholly untrue; yet they can be so cramped and reductive that they miss us altogether: the woman in Capris walking through midtown, the solid-built surgeon off the clock and on his way to a poker game, the plumber casting a fly beside the river—under a dusk-colored slate sky, blank and wordless.
outputs.L3:
The American common is portrayed not as a unified collective with a shared identity, but as a loose network of private needs, desires, habits, and pleasures that intersect in public space. People come together in streets, stores, workplaces, online platforms, and civic institutions, yet they do not necessarily form a single coherent “public.” Instead, they appear as individuals pursuing separate aims, briefly crossing paths with others who are doing the same. What looks like a common culture is therefore made up of countless overlapping personal routines and private motivations.

At the same time, powerful institutions are shown as operating at a distance from ordinary people. Corporations, political organizations, financial systems, media structures, and technological platforms often work secretly or opaquely, making decisions that shape public life without genuine public participation. These institutions tend to view ordinary citizens condescendingly, not as complex individuals, but as manipulable subjects. People are treated as gullible targets: voters to be persuaded, customers to be captured, users to be tracked, or audiences to be managed.

This logic is especially visible in markets and systems of data analysis. Commodities traders, search engines, advertisers, and algorithms translate human behavior into patterns, predictions, and opportunities for profit. In doing so, they reduce people to stereotypes or consumer niches. A person becomes a demographic category, a purchasing tendency, a search history, a risk profile, or a likely political preference. These systems do not need to understand the whole person; they only need enough information to predict or influence behavior.

The text acknowledges that demographic labels and data-driven categories may contain partial truths. Age, income, location, race, gender, education, and browsing habits can reveal something about social experience and collective patterns. However, such categories are always too narrow to capture the full complexity of real human lives. They flatten difference, ignore contradiction, and mistake statistical probability for personal truth. A person may fit a profile in one respect while completely exceeding it in another.

Ultimately, the emphasis falls on the individuality of ordinary people. Their lives cannot be fully explained by the simplified identities imposed on them by institutions, markets, or algorithms. Each person contains private histories, mixed motives, changing desires, loyalties, disappointments, and forms of imagination that resist easy classification. The text therefore challenges systems that claim to know people through data or stereotypes. It insists that ordinary life is richer, stranger, and more complex than the profiles designed to measure, manage, or sell to it.
outputs.L4:
American public life is often described as if it were a spreadsheet. People become “segments,” “markets,” “likely voters,” “urban consumers,” “suburban moms,” “Gen Z shoppers,” “working-class whites,” “Latino men,” “college-educated women,” “high-propensity donors,” “low-information voters,” “early adopters,” “brand-loyal households.” Institutions speak this way because it is useful to them. Political campaigns need targets. Advertisers need audiences. Platforms need profiles. Police departments, insurance companies, retailers, banks, entertainment studios, and news organizations all want to turn the unpredictable crowd into something measurable and manageable.

But the actual crowd refuses to stay inside those labels.

In a bus station, a man in a stained work shirt reads a paperback about medieval theology while eating a vending-machine honey bun. A teenager in rhinestone headphones watches a video about repairing diesel engines. A grandmother with a church hat and immaculate white gloves argues into her phone about cryptocurrency. Two construction workers compare skincare products. A security guard hums an aria under his breath. A woman in a business suit takes off her heels and reveals socks printed with cartoon ghosts. A child in a dinosaur backpack solemnly feeds French fries to a pigeon as if performing a religious rite.

These scenes are ordinary, but they are also strange in the way ordinary life is always strange when observed closely. They do not fit neatly into the categories designed for them. The man is not merely “blue-collar.” The teenager is not merely “youth culture.” The grandmother is not merely “senior consumer.” The woman is not merely “professional female, age 35–49.” Each person carries a dense, private arrangement of habits, memories, loyalties, jokes, fears, tastes, and contradictions. Public life is full of these small unreadable interiors.

Yet powerful systems try to read them anyway. Cameras watch the sidewalk. Phones record location. Loyalty cards remember purchases. Search engines infer anxieties. Streaming services predict desire. Campaign databases assign probabilities to beliefs a person may not even have expressed aloud. The American citizen, shopper, worker, patient, driver, viewer, and voter is constantly being interpreted by machines and institutions that claim to know what kind of person he or she is.

This knowledge is impressive in one sense. It can predict that a person who buys camping equipment may also buy protein bars, or that a household in a certain ZIP code may respond to a certain political message. It can identify patterns invisible to the naked eye. It can place people into categories at tremendous speed and scale. But its power is also its limitation. It sees correlation and mistakes it for character. It sees behavior and mistakes it for identity. It sees the trace a person leaves behind and mistakes that trace for the person.

A mall food court at noon contains more reality than a marketing report can hold. A nurse in scrubs studies a motorcycle catalog. A man wearing a veterans’ cap orders a vegan wrap. A group of high-school girls in identical athletic jackets sit silently together, each absorbed in a different glowing screen. An old couple shares one slice of pizza with the ceremonial gravity of a wedding vow. Nearby, a man at a table covered with shopping bags appears to be asleep, except that he is whispering chess moves to himself. Overhead, a speaker plays a cheerful pop song selected by some corporate office that imagines cheerfulness as a stable atmospheric condition.

The absurdity of such public scenes exposes the poverty of broad cultural generalization. America is constantly explained through types: the heartland, the coast, the consumer, the taxpayer, the base, the swing voter, the immigrant community, the creative class, the forgotten man. These phrases may describe something real at a distance, but they become false when treated as complete. Up close, people overflow their descriptions. They borrow from many cultures at once. They believe incompatible things. They perform one identity at work, another at home, another online, another in memory. They surprise themselves.

The marketplace depends on reducing this complexity. To sell to people efficiently, it must first simplify them. It must decide that a person who bought one thing will want another, that a person of one age will fear one future, that a person from one neighborhood will respond to one image, slogan, or price. Politics does the same. It divides the public into persuadable blocs and mobilizable tribes. Media then repeats the divisions until they begin to feel natural. The result is a country in which people are constantly told who they are by systems that profit from the telling.

Algorithms intensify the problem because they do not merely describe categories; they feed them back to us. A person clicks once, pauses once, buys once, searches once, and the system begins to build a world around that gesture. More of the same appears. The accidental hardens into a preference. The preference becomes a profile. The profile becomes a destiny. A private curiosity turns into a public classification. The individual is surrounded by predictions and then encouraged to become more predictable.

Still, the real person remains partly hidden. This hiddenness is not a failure to be solved. It is one of the conditions of human dignity. No database can fully know why a woman keeps a broken watch in her purse, why a man refuses to eat peaches, why a child is terrified of elevators, why a cashier smiles at one customer and not another, why someone who seems ordinary in every visible way spends the evening building elaborate model ships, writing angry letters never sent, memorizing bird calls, praying, gambling, grieving, or dancing alone in the kitchen.

Surveillance can record movements, but not meanings. Commodification can assign value, but not worth. Demography can count people, but not comprehend them. Cultural analysis can identify tendencies, but not exhaust the lives from which those tendencies are drawn. There is always a remainder: the private joke, the secret shame, the irrational attachment, the inherited song, the dream that has never been spoken, the contradiction that makes a person more than an example of a group.

This is why the public spaces of America, even when ugly or commercialized, still contain a kind of democratic mystery. The airport gate, the laundromat, the DMV, the county fair, the pharmacy line, the interstate rest stop, the fluorescent waiting room—all are filled with people being misread by systems and by one another. A man in camouflage may be a pacifist. A woman with a luxury handbag may be drowning in debt. A student with purple hair may be the most devout person in the room. A quiet janitor may speak four languages. A loud patriot may feel no belonging at all.

The collage of public life defeats the fantasy of total knowledge. Its vividness is an argument. Its absurdity is evidence. People are not clean data points moving through a rational system of consumption and persuasion. They are opaque, theatrical, wounded, comic, stubborn, and unfinished. They live in categories, but they are not contained by them.

The institutions that sort Americans into types will continue to do so, because sorting is profitable and administratively convenient. But the sorted public remains alive beneath the labels. It continues to generate scenes no algorithm would invent: a banker crying at a monster-truck rally, a teenager in a fast-food uniform quoting ancient philosophy, a retired Marine buying glitter glue, a family arguing in three languages over which soda to choose. These moments do not abolish social patterns, but they remind us that patterns are not persons.

To see American life clearly, then, is not to deny data, demographics, or cultural forces. It is to recognize their limits. The map is useful, but the territory is crowded with secrets. Every public face conceals an interior no institution can fully purchase, predict, or possess. The ordinary person, reduced everywhere to a target, remains irreducible.
outputs.L5:
**The American Hugh**

The American Hugh was known for his curiosity, confidence, and restless desire to explore new ideas. Growing up in a country shaped by diversity and ambition, Hugh learned early that success often comes from persistence, creativity, and the courage to take risks. He admired the vast landscapes of America, from busy cities to quiet rural towns, and believed that every place had a story worth telling.

As an American, Hugh valued independence, but he also understood the importance of community. He worked hard to support those around him and believed that progress was strongest when people helped one another. Whether he was speaking with neighbors, traveling across the country, or pursuing his dreams, Hugh carried with him a sense of optimism.

The story of the American Hugh is not just about one person. It represents a broader spirit: the hope to build something meaningful, the freedom to imagine a better future, and the determination to keep moving forward despite challenges.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical prose-poem about “the American common” as a fragmented public made of private desires, advertising categories, airport bars, algorithms, and overlooked ordinary people, in a contemporary satirical style.
counterfactuals.output:
The American common is no pasture but a terminal concourse at 6:17 a.m., blue-lit, carpeted in corporate geometry, where the republic nurses a plastic cup of pale beer beneath a television explaining its feelings in five rotating graphics. Here gather the citizens: Platinum Medallion, Basic Economy, Active Military, Family with Small Children, people temporarily sorted by velocity and debt. Each carries a private weather system—mortgage thunder, custody fog, cholesterol lightning, a secret little sun of want—while the loudspeaker blesses them in mispronounced names.

We have replaced the village green with the demographic segment. Soccer Moms, NASCAR Dads, Gen Z Strivers, Affluent Urban Dog Owners, spiritually homeless but brand-loyal, each grazing in a fenced meadow of predicted preference. The algorithm, our town clerk and rainmaker, knows who is likely to buy a mattress after midnight, who will click on disaster if framed as wellness, who can be nudged from loneliness into a subscription. It hums beneath us like municipal plumbing, carrying away shame and returning it as a coupon.

Still, the common persists—scraped thin, fluorescent, miraculous—in the woman wiping tables at Gate C23, who has heard a thousand men say “I’m sorry” without looking up; in the rideshare driver offering phone chargers like sacraments; in the night stocker arranging cereal boxes into sunrise; in the nurse eating crackers in her parked car; in the boy at the mall kiosk selling screen protectors for devices more tenderly held than children. Their names do not trend. Their faces do not resolve into a marketable concern. They are the background loading endlessly behind the national ad.

O country of checkout prompts and amber waves of liability, of founding documents skimmed between push notifications, of liberty reimagined as customization: choose your own outrage, choose your own insulin plan, choose your own apocalypse colorway. We meet not by meeting but by being tracked in parallel, a confederacy of cookies, our hungers anonymized then auctioned back to us with music. Yet sometimes, in the airport bar, stranded by weather or maintenance or the invisible arithmetic of profit, strangers lean toward one another over fries gone cold and admit the same small defeats. A missed connection. A mother declining. A job that vanished into software. The bartender nods like an unofficial priest.

And for a moment the common flickers—not pure, not pastoral, not saved—only assembled from fatigue and bad coffee, from tip jars and boarding passes, from the stubborn human surplus no category can spend. It is cracked, blinking, overcharged, beautiful by accident. It is everyone waiting to be called, everyone pretending not to listen, everyone listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single long paragraph in the voice of a postmodern American essayist-poet, critiquing consumer profiling and demographic stereotypes while listing surreal groups of citizens in public spaces.
counterfactuals.output: In the republic of bar codes and weather reports, where every citizen is flattened into a purchase likelihood, a neighborhood tendency, a “likely voter,” a “brand loyalist,” a “high-value household,” I keep seeing the actual people overflow the spreadsheet like rainwater over a curb: retirees in silver track shoes arguing with pigeons outside the library; teenagers with glitter on their eyelids and existential dread in their backpacks orbiting the mall fountain; nurses at dawn eating oranges on bus benches; veterans folding receipts into tiny boats; new mothers pushing strollers through the cereal aisle as if navigating a museum of edible propaganda; night-shift janitors with galaxies of bleach on their sleeves; chess-playing uncles in the park who know every regime by its cigarette smoke; delivery cyclists glowing like minor saints in traffic; children in dinosaur pajamas at city hall; accountants in Halloween capes; grandmothers with blue hair feeding parking meters pennies and prayers; undocumented roofers balancing lunch pails and weather systems; poets disguised as substitute teachers; substitute teachers disguised as weathered gods; the lonely, the employed, the overdrawn, the overinsured, the underseen, all moving through plazas and airports and pharmacies and county fairs while the machines whisper: suburban female, urban male, rural swing, luxury aspirant, ethnic segment, anxiety cluster, nostalgia buyer, persuadable moderate, lapsed donor, probable diabetic, outdoor enthusiast, faith-and-family shopper, as though the soul were a coupon clipped from the Sunday insert, as though the human face could be reverse-engineered from a cart containing cat litter, cilantro, batteries, and a birthday candle shaped like the number seven. The insult is not only that the categories are wrong, though they are magnificently wrong, wrong with the confidence of a billboard, wrong with the dead-eyed optimism of a quarterly report; the insult is that they are too small, little shoebox dioramas into which the republic is expected to crawl and pose: “soccer mom,” “angry white man,” “Gen Z activist,” “Black consumer,” “Latino bloc,” “Asian achiever,” “working-class resentment,” “coastal elite,” “heartland values,” “senior fear,” each label a paper hat placed on a burning house. Meanwhile, in the public square, a congregation of tattooed pharmacists releases balloons shaped like extinct currencies; software engineers in thrift-store wedding dresses applaud a busker playing the national anthem on a saw; a choir of warehouse workers chants shipping numbers into the wind; monks with Bluetooth headsets buy pretzels for stray dogs; small-business owners ride escalators holding leeks like ceremonial spears; drag queens and firefighters compare moisturizers beneath a mural of wheat; a man with no fixed address explains Spinoza to a statue; schoolchildren trade stickers of planets that have not yet been discovered; women in courthouse suits smoke beside women in fast-food visors and neither is a demographic, both are weather, both are history, both are improvisations of hunger, memory, rent, tenderness, fury, and the stubborn private jokes that no algorithm can monetize without first murdering them. Consumer profiling pretends to be a mirror, but it is really a net, and a cheap one, the kind sold in bulk to capture butterflies and instead snag plastic bags, church hats, protest signs, grocery lists, unpaid bills, love letters, medical bracelets, bus transfers, and the fragrant steam rising from a paper cup of coffee held by someone who is late for work and thinking of a song her father sang in 1989. To be counted is not the same as to be known; to be targeted is not the same as to be addressed; to be predicted is not the same as to be encountered in the wild light of Tuesday afternoon, standing among the municipal roses with a broken umbrella, a bag of discount plums, and a face too contradictory for any market segment, which is to say: an American face, unfinished, misread, for sale everywhere and finally unavailable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic rant about how corporations, search engines, and political powers reduce Americans to marketing niches, but end by returning to vivid individual figures beneath an unwritten twilight sky.
counterfactuals.output:
They file us by hunger.

Not by the hand that trembles at the mailbox,  
not by the grandmother saving rubber bands in a coffee tin,  
not by the boy in Ohio learning the names of moths  
under a porch light that blinks like a tired star—

but by hunger.

A corporation hears a heartbeat  
and calls it engagement.  
A search engine sees a question  
and sells the shape of the wound.  
A campaign discovers fear in the bloodstream  
and prints it on a banner,  
red, white, blue, and optimized.

They have made a census of our loneliness.  
They have mapped the click, the pause, the glance,  
the midnight search for symptoms,  
the wedding dress saved but never bought,  
the gun ad, the baby formula coupon,  
the debt-relief miracle,  
the “people like you also believed.”

People like you.  
What a small cage  
for a living animal.

They sort us into weatherproof boxes:  
Suburban Anxious. Rural Resentful. Urban Aspirational.  
Mothers Who Worry. Men Who Feel Replaced.  
Patriots. Dreamers. Persuadables.  
High-value households. Low-propensity voters.  
Likely to donate. Likely to despair.  
Likely to scroll until the soul goes numb.

And above us, the engines purr—  
silicon priests in glass towers,  
reading our confessions without absolution.  
They turn memory into inventory,  
grief into demographic,  
rage into a purchasable audience segment.  
They do not need to know our names  
if they can predict the next thing  
we will reach for in the dark.

Meanwhile the powerful arrive smiling,  
wearing flag pins bright as little teeth.  
They speak of freedom  
through rented microphones,  
while the databases bloom behind them  
like black orchards.  
They carve the country into harvestable moods,  
district by district, feed by feed,  
until democracy becomes a focus group  
arguing with its own reflection.

They want America manageable.  
They want the republic broken down  
into flavor profiles.  
They want the soul in a spreadsheet,  
the body in a checkout lane,  
the future in a donor memo,  
the past rewritten as an advertisement  
that follows you from screen to screen  
whispering:  
You chose this.  
You wanted this.  
You are this.

But no.

No algorithm has ever smelled rain  
coming across a soybean field.  
No pollster has ever fully measured  
the silence after a factory whistle stops for good.  
No brand has ever contained  
the whole hot ache of a daughter  
driving all night to reach her father’s bedside.  
No party has ever owned  
the private republic of a kitchen table  
where someone peels an orange  
and offers half without speaking.

Beneath the noise, we remain unwritten.

There is Earl, rinsing grease from his hands  
behind the bus depot, humming Sam Cooke  
to nobody but the dusk.  
There is Marisol, counting tips in the laundromat,  
her child asleep against a basket of warm sheets.  
There is June, ninety-one, painting her nails blue  
because blue was the dress she wore  
when she first kissed a woman in 1954.  
There is DeShawn on the fire escape  
with a cracked astronomy book,  
naming constellations the city refuses to show him.  
There is Abby, at the edge of a wheat field,  
letting her phone die on purpose.  
There is Thomas, who has not forgiven himself,  
standing in the grocery aisle  
holding peaches as if they were fragile planets.

Look—  
the day is lowering its lantern.  
The billboards flicker.  
The feeds refresh.  
The strategists sharpen their maps.

But under an unwritten twilight sky,  
Americans are still walking home:  
each with a face no market can finish,  
each with a sorrow no slogan can own,  
each with a name  
burning softly  
beyond the reach of the machine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose passage using ampersands, long winding sentences, and odd comic details—baton twirlers in red track suits, retirees, evangelical kids, bowlers, nuns, Hugh Grant’s double chin—to meditate on public life in America.
counterfactuals.output:
At the plaza by the municipal fountain, where the water rose & fell with the tired insistence of a committee motion, the baton twirlers in red track suits went wheeling past the retirees on folding chairs, past the evangelical kids with their laminated smiles & clipboards & questions about eternity, past the bowlers in satin league jackets smelling faintly of nachos & lane oil, past the nuns who had come, no one knew why, except perhaps to witness the republic making its daily noise, & all of it seemed to me less like a city than a long sentence refusing to end, inserting comma after comma after comma, as if America itself were an overexplaining uncle at Thanksgiving, breathless, well-meaning, possibly dangerous, waving a roll in one hand & a small flag in the other.

The mayor was late, naturally, because mayors are designed by nature to arrive after the symbolic meaning of an event has already curdled, & while we waited, a man dressed as a colonial cobbler handed out coupons for discounted windshield repair, & a child in a plastic fireman’s helmet asked one of the nuns whether God had ever seen a monster truck, & the nun, who had the calm, lunar face of someone who had survived both Vatican II & dial-up internet, said, “God has seen worse,” which caused one of the bowlers to laugh so hard his rented shoes squeaked on the pavement.

Above us, a banner sagged between two lampposts: COMMUNITY HEALTH & HERITAGE DAY, though nobody could say whose health or which heritage, exactly, since the taco truck was playing yacht rock, the veterans’ booth had run out of pamphlets, the evangelicals had begun debating protein powder with a man in a gorilla costume, & the retirees were conducting, with the grim precision of senators, a referendum on whether the fountain was louder than last year.

This is public life: not the marble speech, not the televised oath, not the clean schoolbook noun glowing in a patriotic haze, but the shared inconvenience of bodies in weather, the civic intimacy of overheard complaints, sunburned necks, folding tables, raffles, hand sanitizer, the old man insisting he once met Hugh Grant in an airport & that Hugh Grant’s double chin was “smaller than you’d think but spiritually present,” the teenage girl twirling a baton high enough to startle a pigeon into flight, the pigeon itself rising like a gray amendment above the plaza, the police cruiser idling beside the kettle corn stand, the minister’s son losing a contact lens near the storm drain & three strangers lowering themselves to the ground to help him find it, all of them suddenly kneeling together in a posture that, from a distance, might have looked like prayer.

& perhaps that is the joke, or the consolation, or the old machinery still turning under the cracked sidewalk: that a country so devoted to privacy keeps inventing occasions to stand too close to one another, to bump elbows over hot dogs, to disagree about traffic cones, to sign petitions we do not read, to be irritated by drums, moved by drums, bored by drums, to watch young women in matching red track suits smile through a routine practiced in gymnasiums & parking lots & mother-haunted minivans, silver batons flashing like little wands of procedural optimism, as if choreography could hold together what argument cannot.

By the time the mayor arrived, waving with the expression of a man who had just misplaced both his notes & his moral authority, the retirees had claimed the shade, the bowlers had formed an accidental honor guard, the nuns were eating lemon ice, the evangelical kids had converted nobody but had acquired several email addresses & a recipe for bean dip, & the fountain continued its bureaucratic splashing, rising & falling, rising & falling, like applause from a crowd that could not quite decide whether the performance was over or whether, against all evidence, the show was still beginning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Whitman-esque but cynical contemporary catalog of American types, blending civic philosophy, media satire, consumer surveillance, and a final quiet image of a plumber fly-fishing at dusk.
counterfactuals.output:
I sing the republic of receipts, the nation of passwords,  
the people indexed, inferred, appended, and sold,  
each citizen haloed by a blue-white screen,  
each hunger translated into a preference,  
each preference into a bid.

I sing the mayor at the ribbon-cutting,  
smiling before the empty factory remade as lofts,  
praising resilience while the eviction notices flower upstairs.

I sing the think-tank fellow, cuffed and quoted,  
explaining liberty as a graph with the poor cropped out.

I sing the anchor, solemn as a courthouse,  
selling fear in measured baritones between commercials  
for pills that may cause dread, numbness, and sudden democracy.

I sing the veteran on hold with the benefits office,  
thirty-seven minutes into the music,  
his patriotism reduced to a case number.

I sing the gig driver circling the airport,  
his bladder disciplined by algorithms,  
his face known to the phone,  
his worth revised every seven seconds.

I sing the teenager whose sadness is A/B tested,  
whose loneliness is a market segment,  
whose laughter is captioned, compressed, and monetized  
before it has fully left the body.

I sing the senator invoking the founders  
beneath a chandelier paid for by men  
who have never waited in line.

I sing the founder too—  
not Jefferson with his lamp, nor Paine with his fire,  
but the man in a fleece vest telling us community  
means agreeing to the terms and conditions.

I sing the school with no librarian,  
the prison with a naming-rights sponsor,  
the hospital where mercy arrives itemized,  
the church livestreaming forgiveness  
beside a button marked Donate Now.

I sing the cop in the cruiser eating alone,  
the protester filmed from three angles,  
the judge elected on a promise to feel nothing,  
the jury instructed to disregard the soul.

I sing the suburbs of identical porches,  
each doorbell awake and suspicious,  
each package photographed like evidence,  
each neighbor both customer and threat.

I sing the farmer whose tractor needs a software license,  
the nurse whose hands remember what policy forgets,  
the cashier asking whether I found everything all right  
in the republic of things no one can find.

I sing the data broker’s invisible harvest—  
pregnancy, panic, debt, desire—  
the intimate weather of the nation  
moving through server farms in Oregon and Virginia,  
cool as a doctrine, humming like bees.

I sing the pundit panel, five heads in boxes,  
debating whether hunger has gone too far,  
whether the people are angry in a productive way,  
whether hope polls better in the Midwest.

I sing the billionaire’s rocket rising  
over tents beneath the overpass,  
the sky briefly privatized,  
the crowd applauding the ascent  
as if gravity itself had been unionized and defeated.

I sing the citizen, myself among them,  
liking the post, hating the system,  
buying the thing, mocking the buyer,  
tracked by the watch that praises my steps  
toward no destination.

O democracy, grand old machine,  
you courthouse hymn, you busted vending machine,  
you promise written in marble and managed by consultants,  
you beautiful unfinished sentence  
sold for parts at auction—

still, somewhere beyond the freeway’s arterial roar,  
past the storage units and the failing mall,  
a plumber in mud-dark boots stands knee-deep in evening water,  
his work truck cooling in the weeds,  
his phone left ringing on the seat,  
and he casts, and waits,  
and the dusk gathers softly around the line.
